    Understanding ovulation and HyPO-P
    A brief patient guide

    What is ovulation?

    Ovulation is when an ovary releases an egg. The egg may enter a fallopian tube and, if fertilized by sperm, results in a pregnancy.

    What is an ovulatory disorder?

    An ovulatory disorder occurs when ovulation does not happen normally. Ovulation may not happen at all, when it is often called anovulation, or it may occur less frequently than normal. It may happen occasionally or continue for months or years.

    What problems can it cause?

    Ovulatory disorders can change menstrual cycles and can make pregnancy more difficult, or, if ovulation is not occurring at all, impossible without medical help.

    How ovulation works

    The hypothalamus and pituitary in the brain coordinate signals to an ovarian follicle. The follicle contains the egg and produces estrogen; after ovulation, progesterone is also produced. These hormones prepare the endometrium for implantation. If pregnancy does not occur, estrogen and progesterone fall and menstruation occurs.

    1 · Hypothalamus

    The hypothalamus sends hormonal signals to the pituitary gland.

    2 · Pituitary

    The pituitary releases hormones that stimulate growth of a follicle in the ovary and contribute to ovulation.

    3 · Follicle and ovary

    The follicle contains the egg and produces estrogen. After ovulation, the ovary also produces progesterone.

    4 · Ovulation

    At ovulation, the egg is released from the ovary and may enter the fallopian tube.

    5 · Endometrium and menstruation

    Estrogen and progesterone prepare the uterine lining for implantation. If pregnancy does not occur, hormone levels fall and a menstrual period occurs.

    Not every absence of ovulation is a disorder

    Ovulation normally does not occur during pregnancy and often during breastfeeding, and it may be intentionally suppressed by hormonal contraception. An ovulatory disorder refers to abnormal ovulatory function outside such expected circumstances.

    What causes ovulatory disorders?

    There are many causes. Some are temporary and return to normal, while others require treatment. Ovulatory dysfunction is common soon after menarche and during the transition toward menopause. Because the causes are so varied, FIGO developed HyPO-P to organize them.

    From PCOS to PMOS in this prototype

    Earlier FIGO patient materials and much of the medical literature use the term PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome). In this prototype, Type IV is termed PMOS (Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovary Syndrome) to emphasize that the syndrome is not confined to the ovary and includes endocrine and metabolic features. PCOS is retained when referring to the historical name or earlier literature; after this explanation, the app uses PMOS.

    Why HyPO-P?

    HyPO-P organizes ovulatory disorders into Type I Hypothalamic, Type II Pituitary, Type III Ovarian, and the separate Type IV PMOS category. This creates a common framework for patients, clinicians, educators, and researchers.

    What happens after the cause is identified?

    Trying to become pregnant

    If infertility is related to an ovulatory disorder, treatment may include medication to induce or restore ovulation, depending on the cause and the individual situation.

    Managing bleeding or other symptoms

    If pregnancy is not the immediate goal, treatment may instead focus on irregular bleeding or associated symptoms such as acne or unwanted hair growth.

    Treating a specific underlying cause

    When a specific cause is identified—such as thyroid dysfunction, a medication effect, or a prolactinoma—treatment can be directed at that cause.

    Patient education adapted from the FIGO patient version v2.2 (2022). Figure 1 reproduced from that patient material.
